narrative:
The model predicted a 71% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. At 25, it sits far below the average of 37 among students who were admitted, signaling weaker preparation for the exam's demands. Your third-year class ranking came next and also increased the likelihood of failure; placing in the 3rd decile is noticeably lower than the 5.8 average among accepted students. These two elements together outweighed the one positive signal in your profile: your first-year ranking in the 5th decile, which slightly improved the outlook but not enough to offset the other concerns.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.4 (versus an admitted average of 3.23), middle-income background, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation, strengthening your academic performance in law school if you retake classes, and considering part-time work options that allow more study time. Reapply once these areas show clear progress. (218 words)
